## 1️⃣ Why the “raw-glyph” server fails for Hindi

When you use the demo URL that ships with the MapLibre starter kit:

```json
"glyphs": "https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"
```

the server simply extracts the *outline* for each Unicode code-point from the TTF/OTF and puts it into a PBF. No **GSUB** (Glyph Substitution) table is consulted, so:

* `क` (U+0915) → rendered correctly.
* `ि` (U+093F) → rendered as a separate glyph that sits **to the right** of the base consonant, because the server never told the renderer “move this vowel sign left of the base”.

Devanagari (and many other Indic scripts) relies on **complex shaping**: a base consonant + vowel sign + possible halant + conjuncts → a single visual glyph cluster. The only way to get that right is to let a shaping engine (HarfBuzz) do the substitution **before** the glyphs are packaged into the PBF.

---

## 2️⃣ Using the open-source Mapbox glyph server (the easiest drop-in)

### 2.1 Install the server

```bash
# Node-based server that ships with Mapbox GL Native
npm install -g @mapbox/fontnik @mapbox/tilelive @mapbox/tilelive-vector @mapbox/tilelive-bridge @mapbox/tilelive-fonts
```

> **Note:** The above installs a *tilelive* pipeline that includes the `tilelive-fonts` plugin – that plugin does the HarfBuzz shaping for you.

### 2.2 Prepare a font directory

Create a folder (e.g. `fonts/`) and drop the Devanagari TTF(s) you want to serve into it:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/glyphs/fonts
cd ~/glyphs/fonts
# Grab the Noto Sans Devanagari regular (or any other Devanagari font)
wget https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/raw/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSansDevanagari/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf
```

You can also add other scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic…) to the same folder – the server will serve any font you place there.

### 2.3 Run the server

```bash
cd ~/glyphs
tilelive copy \
  "bridge://?type=fonts&path=./fonts" \
  "mbtiles://?path=./fonts.mbtiles" \
  --minzoom=0 --maxzoom=14
```

Now start the HTTP endpoint:

```bash
tilelive serve \
  --port 8080 \
  "mbtiles://?path=./fonts.mbtiles"
```

You should see something like:

```
Listening on http://0.0.0.0:8080
```

The server now answers requests of the form:

```
http://localhost:8080/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf
```

and **does** HarfBuzz shaping on the fly.

### 2.4 Point your style at the new server

In your MapLibre style JSON (or in the `MapLibreGL.Map` constructor) replace the `glyphs` line:

```json

  "glyphs": "http://localhost:8080/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  ...
}
```

If you’re using the MapLibre JS API:

```js
const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: {
    version: 8,
    sources: { ... },
    layers:  [ ... ],
    glyphs: 'http://localhost:8080/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf'
  },
  center: [77.2090, 28.6139],
  zoom: 12
});
```

### 2.5 Verify

Zoom in on a Hindi label (e.g. “भारत”). The vowel sign “ा” should now sit **to the right** of the base consonant, and conjuncts like “क्ष” should appear as a single ligature. No more “floating diacritics”.

---

## 3️⃣ Using the MapLibre-GL-Native glyph server (Rust version)

If you prefer a binary with **no Node.js** dependency, the MapLibre GL Native repo ships a tiny glyph server written in Rust.

### 3.1 Build the server

```bash
git clone https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-gl-native.git
cd maplibre-gl-native
cargo build --release --bin glyphs-server
```

The binary will be at `target/release/glyphs-server`.

### 3.2 Prepare fonts

Same as before – put the TTF(s) in a folder, e.g. `~/glyphs/fonts`.

### 3.3 Run

```bash
./target/release/glyphs-server \

  --port 8080

You’ll get a log line:

Listening on http://0.0.0.0:8080
```

Exactly the same URL pattern as the Node server:

```json

```

Same verification steps – Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, etc. should now render correctly.

If you don’t want to run anything locally, you can use a public glyph endpoint that already does shaping.
